source.title: Owner-supplied Mombasa Kutchi grammar elicitation, October 2026
source.citation: Project owner, native-speaker grammaticality judgments and examples, supplied 21 October 2026.
source.notes: Full sentence spellings are retained as supplied. Analyses described as possible or unresolved are not treated as established paradigms.

new_lexemes.meaning: particle in attested object-related, recipient, and experiencer constructions
new_lexemes.note: Its distribution and possible clause-linking use remain under investigation; it is neither universally obligatory nor freely optional.
An oblique demonstrative analysis is a hypothesis; the contrast with hee is attested only in complete constructions.
A distal plural form modifies chokra in one sentence and is translated as they in a desire sentence. Whether these uses have the same grammatical category is unresolved.
Experiencer use is attested; case analysis remains provisional.
Relationship to mere is unresolved and is not assumed here.
Attested with ghar and maru; agreement across all adjectives is not established.
Attested with paani. Held as draft because relation to existing thadh remains for speaker review.
The gloss is inferred from the translation of Hinee ghare(n) me, not separately elicited. Grammatical classification remains open.
Attested in a relative clause; not interchangeable with interrogative ker.
The gloss is inferred from the supplied conditional-sentence translation, not separately elicited. Exact syntactic analysis remains open.

new_lexemes.meaning: negative element in an attested past construction
new_lexemes.note: Distinct attested environment from nah, natho, nathi, nathaa, and nai.

new_lexemes.meaning: negative existential element in an attested expression
new_lexemes.note: Exact grammatical classification remains open; distinct from the other negative forms.

spelling_variants.note: Exact U+2019 spelling in owner-supplied grammatical evidence; same 'why' entry as existing ku'la, with no pronunciation difference established.

forms.note: Speaker-approved in chokre ke kapetho alongside chokro ke kapetho. Form-to-lemma analysis is provisional; case, number, and distribution are unresolved.

examples.note: Native-speaker-approved full construction; paired with Au(n) hee chokro disa(n)tho. Oblique analysis is a hypothesis.
Native-speaker-approved full construction; changing ke coincides with changing hin to hee. Other combinations untested.
Native-speaker-approved alongside chokro ke kapetho. Boy is experiencer; form-to-lemma analysis and distribution of chokre/chokro remain unresolved.
Native-speaker-approved alongside chokre ke kapetho. Boy is experiencer; no obligatory chokre rule.
Whether ghare(n) is plural, oblique, or both is unresolved. Existing hinee=they is not silently assigned this demonstrative use.
Mere has an existing all sense; its exact role here is unresolved.
Existing hinee=they is not silently assigned this demonstrative use.
Maru versus existing maroo remains a held spelling/lexical question.

examples.english: I gave water to the boy.
examples.note: Recipient use of ke; relation of dhinose to a citation lemma remains unconfirmed.
Experiencer use of ke; hin here refers to she and is not merged with demonstrative hin. Kapetho citation lemma unresolved.

examples.kutchi: Mukhe kapetho ke hee chokri hadaa ache
examples.english: I want this girl to come here.
examples.note: Clause-introducing ke is a possible analysis, not a confirmed identity with noun-related ke.
Exact kadho spelling preserved; contrast with attested khadho. Eating verb lemma unresolved.
Plural desire form kape(n)thaa; no parent lemma assigned. Existing hinee=they is not silently assigned this demonstrative use.
Distinct attested plural desire form kape(n)theu(n); distinction from kape(n)thaa unresolved. Hin's plural-context analysis is held.
Eating lemma and kheno analysis unresolved.
Possible masculine singular negative auxiliary agreement remains a hypothesis.
Nathi may reflect feminine negative auxiliary agreement; parent lemma unresolved.
Nathaa may reflect plural agreement; desire lemma unresolved. Existing hinee=they is not silently assigned this demonstrative use.
Attested past negative; na is not treated as interchangeable with nah.
Existing nah=no is preserved; negative imperative use is not silently merged into that sense.
Negative imperative use of nah; existing no sense remains unchanged.
Negative imperative use of nah; existing no sense remains unchanged.

examples.kutchi: Mukhe kheno ai, pun khadho nai
examples.english: I want to eat, but there is no food.
examples.note: Eating lemma unresolved; pun links to the conjunction, not the leaf noun.
Existing hinee=they is not silently assigned this demonstrative use.
Narrow greeting context; no full copula paradigm inferred.

examples.english: How are you? (respected older person; also several people).
examples.note: Two approved contexts for this exact form; no full copula paradigm inferred.
Possessive use of existing mujo=mine is attested but the existing sense is not overwritten.
Possessive jo is attested; existing jo=for is not silently overwritten. Agreement remains untested.

examples.kutchi: Au(n) ghare vina(n)tho se au(n) thake’lo i(n)ya
examples.english: I am going home because I am tired.
examples.note: Full cause construction as supplied; thake’lo analysis unresolved.

examples.kutchi: savare varsaath pondhi, tha poi au(n) ghare rondhose
examples.english: If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.
examples.note: Conditional interpretation is attested; no general if-then construction inferred.

examples.kutchi: Chokro jikee sutho ai, mujo bha ai
examples.english: The boy who is sleeping is my brother.
examples.note: Relative jikee is distinct from interrogative ker; syntactic analysis limited to this sentence.
